hints: Focus on solubility trends down Group 2, they go opposite ways for sulfates and hydroxides, so treat the two tests separately.
Recall that barium sulfate is famously insoluble while magnesium sulfate is very soluble, so test 1 should give much more solid with one ion.
Now flip your thinking for hydroxides, where magnesium hydroxide is insoluble and barium hydroxide is soluble, and compare which ion gives more precipitate in test 2.
walkthrough:
**Recall the Group 2 sulfate trend**

Think solubility of sulfates decreases down the group. That means $\text{MgSO}_4$ is soluble, but $\text{BaSO}_4$ is insoluble.

$$\text{Ba}^{2+}(aq) + \text{SO}_4^{2-}(aq) \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4(s)$$

**Apply to test 1**

Both P and Q get the same amount of $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$. The $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ solution forms a white precipitate of $\text{BaSO}_4$, while the $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ solution stays mostly in solution. So test 1 gives more precipitate with $\text{Ba}^{2+}$.

**Recall the Group 2 hydroxide trend**

Now think the opposite way. Solubility of hydroxides increases down the group. That means $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ is insoluble, but $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$ is soluble.

$$\text{Mg}^{2+}(aq) + 2\text{OH}^{-}(aq) \rightarrow \text{Mg(OH)}_2(s)$$

**Apply to test 2 and conclude**

Both solutions get the same amount of $\text{OH}^{-}$. The $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ solution forms a white precipitate of $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$, while the $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ solution stays mostly in solution. So test 2 gives more precipitate with $\text{Mg}^{2+}$.

options.A: Test 1 is correct for Ba2+, but test 2 is wrong. Ba(OH)2 is soluble, so Ba2+ with NaOH gives little or no precipitate. This choice assumes both trends go the same way down the group.
options.B: Exactly right. Sulfates get less soluble down Group 2, so BaSO4 precipitates more than MgSO4. Hydroxides get more soluble down Group 2, so Mg(OH)2 precipitates more than Ba(OH)2.
options.C: Both parts are reversed. MgSO4 is soluble so it cannot give more precipitate than BaSO4, and Ba(OH)2 is soluble so it cannot give more precipitate than Mg(OH)2. This swaps the two solubility trends.
options.D: Test 2 is correct for Mg2+, but test 1 is wrong. MgSO4 is very soluble, so Mg2+ with Na2SO4 gives little or no precipitate. This choice assumes hydroxides and sulfates follow the same trend.
